title: Colorectal cancer (right colon · left colon · rectum)
scenario: Barium enema shown — apple-core lesion of the ascending colon (a different picture each time, same questions). 430F · 435 · Archive
A 66-year-old man with bleeding per rectum for 3 months; colonoscopy picture shown, biopsy = adenocarcinoma of the descending colon. Archive

Colon-cancer case with symptoms and signs of anaemia; colonoscopy → T3N1 mid-rectal cancer. 439A Patient presented to the clinic with lower GI bleeding (history of colon cancer) → rectal adenocarcinoma. 436F

imgs.cap: Barium enema — apple-core lesion, ascending colon (435 picture) Barium enema — apple-core lesion (arrow) (430F picture)
Another barium enema version + colonoscopy view of the tumour
Colonoscopy — descending-colon cancer (66-year-old with PR bleeding)

qs.q: Take a brief history (bleeding per rectum).
a: Blood: onset, frequency, amount, fresh vs dark, mixed with stool, mucus, painful or painless, change in bowel habit/diarrhoea.
Associated: anaemia symptoms, melaena, abdominal pain/mass, tenesmus, pain on defecation, IBD extra-intestinal features, bleeding elsewhere.
Constitutional: weight loss, appetite loss, fever, fatigue.
Risk factors: family history of colon cancer/IBD, polyps, smoking; PMH (polyps, Crohn's, UC), anticoagulants, previous surgery.
qs.why: Rectal bleeding has benign and malignant causes; the details of the blood (colour, mixed with stool), change in bowel habit, weight loss and family history are what separate cancer from haemorrhoids or colitis.
hist: Blood: onset, frequency, amount
Estimate how much blood has been lost and how chronic the bleeding is.
Fresh vs dark, mixed with stool
Fresh blood separate from stool suggests an anal/distal source; dark blood mixed with stool suggests a more proximal colonic source.
Mucus
Suggests a tumour or inflammatory bowel disease.
Painful or painless
Pain on defecation suggests a fissure; painless bleeding suggests haemorrhoids, a tumour or diverticular bleeding.
Change in bowel habit
A key red-flag symptom of colorectal cancer.
Symptoms of anaemia, melaena
Right-sided colon cancer presents with anaemia rather than visible bleeding.
Abdominal pain or mass, tenesmus
A mass suggests a tumour; tenesmus suggests a rectal lesion.
IBD extra-intestinal features
Joint, eye and skin problems point to inflammatory bowel disease.
Bleeding elsewhere
Suggests a bleeding disorder or anticoagulation.
Weight loss, appetite loss, fever, fatigue
Constitutional symptoms raise the suspicion of malignancy.
Family history, polyps, smoking, IBD
Risk factors for colorectal cancer.
Anticoagulants, previous surgery
Can cause or worsen bleeding and affect planning.

qs.q: What is the type of investigation in this picture?
a: Barium (contrast) enema.
qs.why: Contrast outlining the colon from below on a plain film is a barium (double-contrast) enema.

qs.q: Describe the finding in the picture.
a: Apple-core sign (annular constricting lesion) in the ascending colon.
qs.why: An annular tumour narrows the lumen with shouldered, irregular edges — the "apple-core" appearance.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
a: Right-sided colon cancer.
qs.why: An apple-core stricture in the ascending colon is a colon carcinoma until biopsy proves otherwise.

qs.q: What are the possible symptoms for such patients?
a: Iron-deficiency anaemia (unrecognised blood loss — commoner in right-sided cancer): SOB, fatigue, palpitations.
Melaena, weight loss, right lower-quadrant pain/mass.
qs.why: The right colon is wide with liquid stool, so tumours bleed occultly and rarely obstruct — they present with iron-deficiency anaemia, a mass or weight loss.

qs.q: What investigations will you order?
a: Labs: CBC, U&E, LFT, coagulation profile, CEA.
Diagnostic: colonoscopy + biopsy.
Staging: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (+ MRI pelvis for rectal cancer).
Follow-up for recurrence: CEA, CBC, renal profile, LFT.
qs.why: Colonoscopy with biopsy gives the diagnosis and checks for synchronous tumours; CT chest/abdomen/pelvis stages it (MRI for rectal); CEA is a baseline for follow-up.

qs.q: The biopsy shows adenocarcinoma of the descending colon — what will you do next?
a: Prepare the patient for left hemicolectomy (after staging).
qs.why: A descending colon cancer is removed by a left hemicolectomy (with its lymphatic drainage), after staging shows it is resectable.

qs.q: What are the stages of colon cancer?
a: Stage 0: carcinoma in situ (mucosa only).
Stage I: T1–T2 (submucosa, muscularis propria).
Stage II: T3–T4 (full thickness / adjacent organs).
Stage III: any lymph-node involvement.
Stage IV: distant metastases.
qs.why: TNM groups: depth of the wall (T) gives stages I–II, any node involvement makes it stage III, and distant spread stage IV.

qs.q: What is the treatment for this patient?
a: Stage I: right hemicolectomy.
Stage II: right hemicolectomy ± adjuvant chemo (if high risk).
Stage III: right hemicolectomy + adjuvant chemo.
Stage IV: chemotherapy ± palliative surgery.
qs.why: Surgery removes the tumour and its nodes; chemotherapy is added when nodes are involved (or in high-risk stage II) to kill micrometastases; stage IV is mainly systemic.

qs.q: In which stage do we use chemotherapy?
a: All stage III (node-positive), stage IV, and high-risk stage II.
qs.why: Adjuvant chemotherapy benefits patients with a high risk of systemic recurrence: node-positive (III), metastatic (IV) and high-risk II.

qs.q: What do you mean by high-risk stage II?
a: Young patient, presented with obstruction (or perforation), positive family history, lympho- vascular invasion, inadequate surgery (< 12 lymph nodes).
qs.why: These features predict recurrence in node-negative disease (or mean the node status is unreliable when < 12 nodes were examined), so chemotherapy is offered.

qs.q: Mention the surgical treatment without staging (in general), and explain how to do a right hemicolectomy on the same X-ray.
a: Right hemicolectomy — point to the ascending colon (resected segment) and mention the ileo- colic anastomosis.
qs.why: The resection follows the blood supply and lymphatics of the ascending colon (ileocolic, right colic, right branch of middle colic), ending with an ileocolic anastomosis.

qs.q: Rectal cancer is T3–T4 / T3N1 mid-rectum — how would you manage it?
a: Neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy → surgery (TME) ± adjuvant chemotherapy.
qs.why: Locally advanced mid/low rectal cancer has a high local recurrence risk — neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy shrinks it before total mesorectal excision.

qs.q: What is the name of the surgery? (rectal cancer)
a: (Low) anterior resection.
qs.why: Rectal cancers above the sphincters are removed by (low) anterior resection with TME, preserving the anus.

qs.q: How would you prepare the patient for hemicolectomy?
a: Consent (incl. possible stoma), bowel preparation (mechanical ± oral antibiotics), DVT prophylaxis, general pre-op work-up.
qs.why: Preparation lowers the risks of surgery: informed consent (including a possible stoma), bowel prep to reduce infection, and DVT prophylaxis in a cancer patient.

qs.q: What is colonic preparation?
a: Clearing the colon of stool and organisms: mechanical (osmotic laxative, e.g. PEG "Colyte" — empties the colon in 3–4 h) + microbial (oral metronidazole/antibiotics). Small bowel needs no preparation.
qs.why: Colonic contents carry a heavy bacterial load; emptying the bowel mechanically and reducing bacteria with oral antibiotics lowers wound infection and leak.

qs.q: What are the complications of the surgery?
a: Bleeding, anastomotic leak, infection, perforation, injury to surrounding structures (ureter, small bowel, liver, spleen).
qs.why: General surgical complications (bleeding, infection) plus the specific ones of bowel surgery — anastomotic leak and injury to nearby organs.

qs.q: Mention a specific complication that usually results from iatrogenic injury during the operation.
a: Splenic injury, ureteric injury.
qs.why: Mobilising the splenic flexure can tear the splenic capsule; the left ureter lies close to the sigmoid/descending mesentery and can be injured.

qs.q: How will you follow up the patient?
a: History, exam, CBC, LFT and CEA every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months for 3 years. Colonoscopy and CT after 1 year, then annually for 5 years; after 5 clear years, average-risk screening (colonoscopy every 5–10 years).
qs.why: Most recurrences occur in the first 2–3 years, so follow-up is closest then: CEA, imaging and colonoscopy detect recurrence or new tumours while they are still treatable.

title: Anal fissure
scenario: A picture of an anal fissure. 438A · 441A · Archive

imgs.cap: Anal fissure — diagrams and clinical photo

qs.q: Describe what you see.
a: A longitudinal (vertical) tear in the posterior midline of the lower anal canal.
qs.why: Describe position and shape: a longitudinal tear in the posterior midline of the anoderm (below the dentate line).

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Anal fissure.
qs.why: A posterior midline linear split = anal fissure.

qs.q: What are the causes?
a: Constipation & straining (hard stool), diarrhoea, high sphincter tone; secondary: Crohn's, cancer, STIs, TB, childbirth.
qs.why: Passage of hard stool tears the anoderm; high sphincter tone reduces blood flow to the posterior midline so it fails to heal. Off-midline fissures suggest secondary causes.

qs.q: What signs and symptoms might the patient have?
a: Severe pain with defecation, bright red blood on the toilet paper, increased sphincter tone; exam: visible tear, extreme pain on PR.
qs.why: The anoderm is richly innervated (below the dentate line) — hence severe pain on defecation with a little bright red blood; spasm makes PR very painful.

qs.q: Describe the features of a chronic fissure (3 features in the picture).
a: Hypertrophied anal papilla, sentinel pile (skin tag), the fissure itself with visible internal- sphincter fibres.
qs.why: Chronicity shows as a sentinel tag at the outer end, a hypertrophied papilla at the inner end, and exposed internal sphincter fibres in the base.

qs.q: What is the medical (conservative) treatment?
a: Treat constipation: water, fibre, stool softeners/bulk-forming agents; sitz baths; analgesia (local anaesthetic, ibuprofen).
Relax the sphincter: topical GTN or diltiazem for 8–12 weeks (they focused on GTN); if it fails → Botox injection.
qs.why: Softening stool stops re-tearing, and relaxing the internal sphincter (GTN/diltiazem, then Botox) improves blood flow so the fissure heals.

qs.q: What if conservative therapy fails? (surgical treatment)
a: Lateral internal sphincterotomy.
qs.why: Dividing part of the internal sphincter permanently lowers the tone — the most effective cure, at a small risk of incontinence.

qs.q: What is the DDx of a fissure in the lateral wall?
a: Crohn's disease, anal-canal cancer, STIs.
qs.why: Lateral or multiple fissures are atypical — think Crohn's, cancer, STIs or TB, and examine under anaesthesia with biopsy.

tips.t: According to Dr Al-Turaiki the first three (visible sphincter fibres, hypertrophied papilla, sentinel pile) are the answers to give; know how to point to each in a real picture.

title: Adhesive small-bowel obstruction
scenario: A patient presented to the ER with acute abdominal pain and distension; appendectomy 6 months / 1 year / 2 years ago. The examiner asks about ER management, then shows an erect abdominal X-ray. 430A · 430F · Old exam Small-bowel obstruction — X-ray shown. 441F

imgs.cap: Abdominal X-ray (supine) — dilated small-bowel loops Erect abdominal X-ray — multiple central air-fluid levels
Official answer sheet photographed in the 430 exam

qs.q: Take a focused history.
a: Pain history (SOCRATES) + vomiting (bilious/faeculent), distension, last flatus/bowel motion (obstipation), previous surgery, hernias, weight loss / change in bowel habit.
qs.why: The cardinal features of obstruction (pain, vomiting, distension, obstipation) and the cause (previous surgery = adhesions, hernias, cancer).
hist: Pain (SOCRATES)
Colicky pain = obstruction; constant, severe pain suggests strangulation.
Vomiting (bilious/faeculent)
Early bilious vomiting = proximal obstruction; faeculent vomiting = distal/late obstruction.
Distension
More marked in distal obstruction.
Last flatus / bowel motion
Absolute constipation (obstipation) confirms complete obstruction.
Previous surgery
Adhesions are the commonest cause of small-bowel obstruction.
Hernias
The second commonest cause — always check the hernial orifices.
Weight loss / change in bowel habit
Raises suspicion of a tumour causing the obstruction.

qs.q: How would you manage this patient in the ER?
a: NPO + NGT (decompression, prevents aspiration).
IV fluids; Foley catheter (input/output).
Bloods: CBC, U&E, cross-match, coagulation profile, ABG, LDH; correct electrolytes. Erect chest X-ray + abdominal X-ray; consider early broad-spectrum antibiotics.
qs.why: "Drip and suck": NG decompression, fluids and electrolyte correction (patients are dehydrated from vomiting and third-spacing), catheter to monitor output.

qs.q: What investigations will you order?
a: Labs as above + erect & supine AXR, erect CXR; CT abdomen if unclear.
qs.why: Bloods show dehydration and ischaemia (lactate, WBC); films confirm obstruction; CT finds the cause and signs of strangulation.

qs.q: What do you see in the image?
a: Multiple central air-fluid levels with dilated small-bowel loops.
qs.why: Multiple air-fluid levels in dilated central loops with valvulae conniventes are small-bowel obstruction.

qs.q: What type of X-ray is this?
a: Plain abdominal X-ray, erect (and supine).
qs.why: Fluid levels are seen only on an erect (horizontal-beam) film; the supine film shows the loop pattern.

qs.q: What is your most likely diagnosis?
a: Adhesive (small-bowel) intestinal obstruction.
qs.why: Previous abdominal surgery + SBO picture = adhesive obstruction (the commonest cause).

qs.q: What are the causes, and the most common cause?
a: Small bowel: Adhesions (most common) › Bulge (hernia) › Cancer. Large bowel: cancer › diverticulitis › volvulus.
qs.why: Adhesions cause most SBO; hernias next. In the large bowel, cancer leads, then diverticular disease and volvulus.

qs.q: What are the symptoms?
a: Colicky pain, vomiting, distension, obstipation.
qs.why: Colicky pain from peristalsis against the block, vomiting, distension and absolute constipation.

qs.q: What are the indications for surgical intervention in this patient?
a: Abdominal tenderness / guarding (strangulation), pneumoperitoneum, complete obstruction, failure of conservative management (~3 days — ask about passing flatus/stool).
qs.why: Signs of strangulation or perforation, complete obstruction, or failure of 48–72 h of conservative treatment mean surgery.

qs.q: Which study is both diagnostic and therapeutic?
a: Water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) follow-through: contrast in the colon by 24 h predicts resolution and may speed it up.
qs.why: Gastrografin is hyperosmolar — it draws fluid into the bowel and may relieve the obstruction, and its arrival in the colon predicts success.

extra.q: What are the classic electrolyte and acid–base findings in proximal obstruction?
a: Hypovolaemia, hypochloraemia, hypokalaemia, metabolic alkalosis. (High LDH & metabolic acidosis suggest ischaemia; pneumobilia suggests gallstone ileus.)
Post-operative ileus, metabolic (DKA, ↓Na, ↓K, ↓Mg, ↑Ca), drugs (opioids), sepsis, pneumonia, renal stone, retroperitoneal haematoma, spine/rib fractures, vascular occlusion.

title: Bloody diarrhoea (IBD) & lower GI bleeding
scenario: A 30-year-old woman with abdominal pain and bloody diarrhoea. Old exam
A woman in her 30s with painless bloody diarrhoea (lower GI bleeding). 435 · Archive

imgs.cap: Indications for surgery in Crohn's disease (summary box)

qs.q: What are the important points in the history?
a: Diarrhoea/blood: onset, frequency, volume, fresh vs dark, mucus, oily stool, pain, tenesmus, incomplete emptying; food/water, travel, sick contacts.
Associated: obstruction (pain, distension, vomiting, constipation), abdominal mass, perianal disease, IBD extra-intestinal features, bleeding elsewhere.
Constitutional symptoms; risk factors for colon cancer; PMH (polyps, IBD); drugs
(anticoagulants, laxatives, antibiotics); family history (colon cancer, IBD); smoking.
qs.why: The history separates infection (travel, contacts), inflammation (IBD: young, diarrhoea, extra-intestinal features), ischaemia and neoplasia (older, weight loss, bowel-habit change).
hist: Diarrhoea/blood: onset, frequency, volume
Severity of the colitis and of the fluid and blood loss.
Fresh vs dark, mucus
Blood and mucus point to colitis (IBD or infection).
Oily stool
Suggests malabsorption.
Pain, tenesmus, incomplete emptying
Tenesmus and incomplete emptying mean rectal involvement.
Food/water, travel, sick contacts
Infective diarrhoea must be excluded first.
Obstruction symptoms (pain, distension, vomiting, constipation)
Strictures in Crohn's or a tumour can obstruct.
Abdominal mass, perianal disease
A right iliac fossa mass and perianal fistulae/abscesses suggest Crohn's.
IBD extra-intestinal features
Arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, PSC support IBD.
Bleeding elsewhere
Points to a bleeding disorder.
Constitutional symptoms, colon cancer risk factors
Cancer is a differential and a long-term risk in IBD.
Anticoagulants, laxatives, antibiotics
Antibiotics → C. difficile; laxatives → diarrhoea; anticoagulants → bleeding.
Family history (colon cancer, IBD), smoking
Genetic tendency; smoking worsens Crohn's (and is protective in UC).

qs.q: What is your differential diagnosis? (mention ≥ 10)
a: Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, infectious colitis (incl. pseudomembranous), ischaemic colitis, colon cancer, polyps, angiodysplasia, diverticular disease, haemorrhoids, anal fissure, massive upper GI bleed.
qs.why: Bloody diarrhoea/LGIB covers inflammatory, infective, ischaemic, neoplastic, vascular and anorectal causes — and a brisk upper GI bleed can also present with red blood.

qs.q: How would you examine this patient?
a: Abdominal examination + rectal examination with proctoscopy.
qs.why: Abdominal exam finds tenderness/masses; PR and proctoscopy see the anal canal and rectum, where many bleeding sources lie.

qs.q: How would you investigate this patient?
a: Bloods: CBC, U&E, LFT, CRP/ESR, folate/B12, coagulation, cross-match, CEA; stool cultures.
Imaging: AXR, CT; colonoscopy + biopsy (if it fails → angiography).
qs.why: Bloods measure blood loss and inflammation; stool cultures exclude infection; colonoscopy with biopsy distinguishes UC, Crohn's, ischaemia and cancer.

qs.q: What are the indications for surgery in Crohn's / IBD?
a: Failure of medical treatment, toxic megacolon, acute haemorrhage, perforation, obstruction, abscess, fistula, carcinoma (development/prevention).
qs.why: IBD is medical first; surgery is for failure of medicine or complications (megacolon, perforation, bleeding, obstruction, fistula, abscess, dysplasia/cancer).

qs.q: Colonoscopy failed because of bleeding — what will you do next?
a: CT angiography (Dr Mufti & Dr Al-Turaiki) — tagged RBC scan is an alternative.
qs.why: When active bleeding obscures colonoscopy, CT angiography localises the bleeding point (needs ~0.5 mL/min) and guides embolisation.

qs.q: How would you manage lower GI bleeding?
a: Classify as stable/unstable (vitals, labs, urine output) and resuscitate.

Unstable: 2 large-bore IV lines, resuscitation, Foley catheter (urine output ≈ 0.5 mL/kg/h). Exclude an upper GI source with an NG tube (± OGD), then colonoscopy → CT angiography / angio-embolisation → surgery if still bleeding.
qs.why: Resuscitate first; exclude an upper GI source (it can present as LGIB); then localise and treat — colonoscopy, then angiography/embolisation, and surgery only if bleeding persists.

title: Sigmoid volvulus
scenario: An old man with signs of large-bowel obstruction. 439F
An abdominal X-ray is shown. Archive

qs.q: What is your differential diagnosis?
a: Malignancy (colon cancer), sigmoid volvulus.
qs.why: Large-bowel obstruction in an elderly patient is commonly from colon cancer or sigmoid volvulus.

qs.q: What investigation will you order?
a: Plain abdominal X-ray.
qs.why: A plain abdominal film shows the dilated colon and often a diagnostic pattern.

qs.q: What are the findings?
a: Plain abdominal radiograph showing the characteristic "coffee-bean" sign — a hugely dilated loop of large bowel.
qs.why: A massively distended loop arising from the pelvis, folded on itself, gives the "coffee-bean" sign.

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Sigmoid volvulus.
qs.why: A coffee-bean loop with LBO in an elderly patient is sigmoid volvulus.

qs.q: What is the management?
a: Stable, first time: endoscopic detorsion (rigid/flexible sigmoidoscopy) and a large-bore rectal (flatus) tube left for ~48 h (the doctor concentrated on it).
Then elective sigmoid colectomy after bowel prep (curative in the fit patient).
Unstable / peritonitis / gangrene → emergency surgery.
qs.why: Endoscopic detorsion relieves the obstruction without surgery and a rectal tube prevents early re-twisting; because recurrence is common, elective sigmoid colectomy follows. Gangrene or peritonitis needs emergency resection.

title: Anal fistula
scenario: A picture of the perianal area with an external opening. 437A · 438F · 439B

imgs.cap: Anal fistula — external opening Anal fistula — bubbles at the internal opening

qs.q: What do you see in the picture?
a: Anal fistula (external opening).
qs.why: An opening on the perianal skin draining pus/discharge is the external opening of a fistula-in-ano.

qs.q: What are the types (classification) of fistula?
a: Parks: intersphincteric, trans-sphincteric, suprasphincteric, extrasphincteric.
qs.why: Parks' classification is by the tract's relation to the sphincters — it decides how much muscle a cure would cut.

qs.q: What are the aetiologies / risk factors?
a: Perianal abscess / infected anal crypt gland (most common), Crohn's disease, TB, malignancy, trauma, previous surgery/radiotherapy, immunocompromise (HIV).
qs.why: Most fistulas follow an abscess from an infected anal gland (cryptoglandular); recurrent or complex ones suggest Crohn's, TB or malignancy.

qs.q: Explain Goodsall's rule.
a: Draw a transverse line across the anal verge: an external opening anterior to the line → straight radial tract; posterior → curved tract opening in the posterior midline.
qs.why: Goodsall's rule predicts the internal opening from the external one so the surgeon can find the tract.

qs.q: Mention 2 investigations you will do.
a: Endo-anal ultrasound and MRI pelvis (fistulogram).
qs.why: Endoanal US and MRI define the tract and its relation to the sphincters before surgery.

qs.q: The patient has a low-lying fistula — what is the management?
a: Fistulotomy.
qs.why: A low fistula involves little sphincter, so laying it open (fistulotomy) cures it without incontinence.

qs.q: What is the difference between fistulotomy and fistulectomy?
a: Fistulotomy lays open the tract; fistulectomy excises (removes) the tract.
qs.why: Fistulotomy opens the tract and lets it heal from the base; fistulectomy cuts out the whole tract (larger wound).

title: Diverticulitis
scenario: A 60-year-old man presents to the ER with left lower-quadrant pain; vitally stable, no signs of peritonitis. (new case) 442A · 442B

qs.q: What imaging modality would you order?
a: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast (full answer needed).
qs.why: CT with contrast confirms diverticulitis and grades it (phlegmon, abscess, perforation), which decides treatment.

qs.q: What features would you see on the CT?
a: Pericolic fat stranding, bowel-wall thickening/inflammation, phlegmon, abscess.
qs.why: Inflammation around the diverticulum shows as fat stranding and wall thickening; complications as abscess or free gas.

qs.q: CT shows a 1 cm pericolic abscess — what is the management?
a: Admit; NPO, NGT, IV fluids, analgesia and IV antibiotics (small abscess < 3–4 cm → antibiotics alone).
qs.why: A small (< 3–4 cm) abscess usually resolves with IV antibiotics; larger ones need percutaneous drainage.

qs.q: Mention 4 criteria to admit the patient.
a: Old age, vitally unstable / sepsis, signs of peritonitis, poor social support, immunosuppression (also inability to tolerate oral intake, significant comorbidity).
qs.why: Patients who are elderly, septic, peritonitic, immunosuppressed, can't take orally or lack support need admission; others can be treated as outpatients.

title: Acute appendicitis (adult)
scenario: A 23-year-old man with RLQ pain for 8 hours. Archive

qs.q: Take a brief history.
a: Pain: started periumbilical then shifted to RLQ, onset, character, radiation, aggravating/relieving, severity.
Associated: anorexia, N/V, diarrhoea/constipation, urinary symptoms (renal stone), fever.
Female: LMP, pregnancy (ectopic), gynaecological symptoms. PMH, drugs, surgery, family & social history.
qs.why: The classic story is periumbilical pain shifting to the RLQ with anorexia and vomiting; in women always ask about LMP/pregnancy and gynaecological symptoms.
hist: Pain started periumbilical, shifted to RLQ
Early visceral pain is felt at the umbilicus (midgut); it moves to the RLQ when the parietal peritoneum is inflamed — the classic appendicitis story.
Onset, character, radiation, severity
Complete the pain assessment and help separate appendicitis from other causes.
Anorexia, nausea, vomiting
Anorexia is very common in appendicitis; vomiting usually follows the pain.
Diarrhoea/constipation
Diarrhoea first suggests gastroenteritis; a pelvic appendix can irritate the rectum.
Urinary symptoms
Exclude renal stone and UTI (a pelvic appendix can also cause dysuria).
Fever
Low-grade fever supports appendicitis; high fever suggests perforation.
LMP, pregnancy, gynaecological symptoms
Ectopic pregnancy, ovarian torsion/cyst and PID are key differentials in women.
PMH, drugs, surgery
Previous appendicectomy excludes the diagnosis; comorbidities matter for surgery.

qs.q: What is your differential diagnosis?
a: Acute appendicitis, Crohn's disease, renal colic, Meckel's diverticulum, gynaecological causes in females (ectopic, ovarian torsion/cyst, PID).
qs.why: RLQ pain mimics include urological, gynaecological and other bowel causes — they must be excluded.

qs.q: What is the diagnosis?
a: Acute appendicitis.
qs.why: Migratory pain to the RLQ with anorexia, fever and RLQ tenderness is acute appendicitis.

qs.q: What are the findings on examination?
a: RLQ (McBurney's point) tenderness, guarding/rigidity, rebound tenderness; Rovsing's, psoas and obturator signs.
qs.why: Peritoneal irritation over the appendix gives McBurney's tenderness and rebound; Rovsing's, psoas and obturator signs reflect its position.

qs.q: What investigations will you order?
a: Clinical diagnosis; CBC (leukocytosis); US first (MRI if pregnant and US inconclusive); CT.
qs.why: It's a clinical diagnosis supported by WBC; US first (no radiation), CT in adults when unsure, MRI in pregnancy.

qs.q: What is your management?
a: ABC, NPO, NGT if vomiting, 2 large-bore IV lines, bloods, IV fluid bolus, IV antibiotics, analgesia, Foley/monitor output.
Laparoscopic appendectomy.
qs.why: Resuscitate, give antibiotics, then remove the appendix — laparoscopic appendectomy is the standard.

qs.q: What are the 2 groups of organisms, and an appropriate antibiotic for each?
a: Gram-negative bacteria → cefuroxime; anaerobes → metronidazole.
qs.why: Appendicitis is a mixed gut infection — Gram-negatives (E. coli) need a cephalosporin and anaerobes (Bacteroides) need metronidazole.

qs.q: If left untreated for 5 days, what complications might develop?
a: Perforation & peritonitis, appendicular mass, appendicular abscess, portal pyaemia
(pylephlebitis), paralytic ileus.
qs.why: Untreated, the appendix perforates; the body may wall it off (mass/abscess) or infection spreads (peritonitis, portal pyaemia).

qs.q: If he presents late, how do you know if he has an abscess or a mass?
a: CT scan.
qs.why: CT distinguishes a phlegmon/mass (inflammatory) from an abscess (drainable collection).

qs.q: CT shows an abscess — what will you do?
a: CT/US-guided percutaneous drainage + antibiotics (interval appendectomy later).
qs.why: An abscess is drained percutaneously with antibiotics, avoiding a difficult operation in inflamed tissue; interval appendectomy is considered later.

qs.q: What complication might happen during the operation?
a: Perforation of the caecum.
qs.why: An inflamed, friable caecal base can tear or the stump can leak.

tips.t: Don't forget WIPER (wash hands, introduce, permission, expose, reposition) and the named signs.

bonus.stem: A 30-year-old man has fever, RLQ pain and a palpable tender mass. CT shows a 6 cm appendiceal abscess. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: B. Laparoscopy to drain the abscess and remove the appendix
C. IV antibiotics and image-guided percutaneous drainage

qs.q: What is this?
a: A stoma.
qs.why: A segment of bowel brought out through the abdominal wall is a stoma.

qs.q: What kind of stoma?
a: Colostomy (because it is flat; an ileostomy is spouted).
qs.why: Colostomies are made flush with the skin (formed stool, less irritant); ileostomies are spouted so the irritant liquid effluent drops into the bag away from the skin.

qs.q: What are the indications?
a: Removal of the distal colon with the anal canal (abdominoperineal resection), anal canal tumours, complicated diverticular disease, protection of an anastomosis, perianal fistula.
qs.why: A stoma diverts faeces when the distal bowel/anus is removed (APR) or when a distal anastomosis or diseased segment needs protecting.

qs.q: What are the complications?
a: Ischaemia/necrosis, retraction, parastomal hernia, prolapse (also stenosis, skin irritation).
qs.why: Poor blood supply causes necrosis, tension causes retraction, and the abdominal-wall opening allows a parastomal hernia or prolapse.

qs.q: What are the types of stoma?
a: Anatomical: colostomy, ileostomy, gastrostomy, jejunostomy · Duration: temporary or permanent
· Loop vs end.
qs.why: Stomas are classified by the organ, by intent (temporary vs permanent) and by construction (loop vs end).
